passage_text: Researchers investigated the impact of sleep deprivation on short‑term memory performance in healthy adults. A total of 120 participants (aged 18–35) were randomly assigned to either a control group (normal sleep) or a sleep‑deprived group (restricted to 4 hours of sleep per night for two nights). After the intervention, all subjects completed a standardized word‑list recall test. The data are summarized in Table 1. The study aimed to determine whether reduced sleep leads to measurable deficits in memory retrieval and to assess the magnitude of this effect. The researchers also collected demographic variables (age, sex, baseline cognitive score) to control for potential confounders. The results were intended to inform workplace policies and public health recommendations regarding sleep hygiene.
table_data:
Table 1. Memory Test Scores by Group

Group | N | Mean Score (SD)
Control | 60 | 85.4 (7.2)
Sleep‑Deprived | 60 | 72.1 (9.5)
stem: Which of the following best describes the main finding of the study?

options.A: Sleep deprivation had no effect on memory performance.
options.C: The mean memory score was lower in the sleep-deprived group than in the control group.
options.D: The study could not determine the effect of sleep deprivation.

explanation: Correct: The sleep-deprived mean (72.1) is lower than the control mean (85.4). Why the others are wrong: A) a 13.3-point gap in means is not 'no effect'. B) scores were lower, not higher, after sleep deprivation. D) the study reported data from both groups, so a difference between them can be described.
trap: Choosing D or A because no p-value is shown, although the table still reports a clear 13.3-point gap in means.

stem: Which experimental design best matches the study’s methodology?
explanation: Participants were randomly assigned to two conditions (control vs. sleep‑deprived) and then measured on the same outcome, which is the hallmark of a randomized controlled trial.
trap: Calling the study cross-sectional because memory was measured only once, overlooking that investigators randomly assigned the sleep condition.

stem: Calculate the absolute difference in mean memory scores between the two groups.
explanation: Correct: C) Absolute difference = 85.4 - 72.1 = 13.3 points. Why the others are wrong: A) 5.3 does not follow from the table values. B) 7.2 is the control group's SD, not a difference in means. D) 16.7 adds the two SDs (7.2 + 9.5) instead of subtracting the means.
trap: Adding the two standard deviations (7.2 + 9.5 = 16.7) or quoting a single SD instead of subtracting the group means.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by Table 1?

options.A: The control group's mean score exceeded the sleep-deprived group's by 13.3 points.
options.C: Scores varied more among sleep-deprived participants than among controls.
options.D: The sleep-deprived group's scores were less variable than the control group's.

explanation: Correct: The sleep-deprived SD (9.5) is larger than the control SD (7.2), so its scores were more, not less, variable. Why the others are wrong: A) 85.4 − 72.1 = 13.3. B) N = 60 for each group. C) 9.5 is greater than 7.2.
trap: Assuming the lower-scoring group must also be the less variable one.

stem: The pooled SD of the two groups is about 8.4 points. About how many pooled SDs is the difference in mean scores?
explanation: Correct: C) 13.3 / 8.4 is about 1.6 pooled SDs. Why the others are wrong: A) 0.6 would correspond to a difference of about 5 points. B) 1.4 divides by the larger group SD (9.5) instead of the pooled SD. D) 2.4 would correspond to a difference of about 20 points.
trap: Dividing the 13.3-point difference by the larger group SD (9.5) gives 1.4 (B) rather than using the pooled SD of 8.4.
